extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating claim language and claim format (functional limitations, Markush groups, negative limitations, multiplicity, product-by-process, use claims, omnibus claims, references to figures/tables, etc.) for compliance with 35 U.S.C. §112 and related requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to another claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to limitations recited in another claim is not per se indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph; e.g., reference to 'the nozzle of claim 7' was held to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While cross-referencing other claims is permissible, if the format of making reference to limitations recited in another claim results in confusion, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph) is proper. See Ex parte Porter, 25 USPQ2d 1144 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1992).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining a dependent claim, the examiner should determine whether the claim complies with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA fourth paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 608.01(n), subsection II for procedures and details on dependent claim treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations — general permissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language (reciting a feature 'by what it does rather than by what it is') is not inherently wrong and may be employed; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-/step-plus-function) expressly authorizes a form of functional claiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language often involves reciting some structure followed by its function and may be permissible (e.g., conical spout that 'allow[ed] several kernels…to pass through'), but must be evaluated like any other limitation for what it fairly conveys to a person of ordinary skill in the art in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations — when they are indefinite or unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language may fail to provide a clear-cut indication of scope when it merely describes a problem to be solved or a result achieved, or when it lacks particular structure/materials/steps that accomplish the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlimited functional claim limitations that extend to all means or methods of resolving a problem may be indefinite or lack written description/enablement support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Courts cited: Swinehart, Halliburton, United Carbon, Ariad, Hyatt, Datamize. Examples: claiming a device as merely 'aesthetically pleasing' or reciting only a desired result without structure can be indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to determine ambiguity of functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether (1) there is a clear-cut indication of the scope of subject matter covered by the claim; (2) the language sets forth well-defined boundaries of the invention or only states a problem/result; and (3) a person of ordinary skill would know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are examples and not exhaustive; relevance may vary by art. The primary inquiry is whether the language leaves room for ambiguity or whether the boundaries are clear and precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to resolve ambiguity of functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, applicant may resolve ambiguities by e.g., using quantitative metrics, providing specification formulas/examples, providing general guidelines and examples, or amending claims to recite particular structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) numeric limitation as to a physical property; (2) specification providing a formula and examples that meet/do not meet the limitation (Oakley example); (3) general guidelines and examples sufficient to teach POSITA (Marosi example); (4) amend to recite particular structure that accomplishes the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush group (alternatives) — closed vs open grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives (selected from the group 'consisting of' the listed members). If a Markush grouping requires selection from an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2117 and Supplementary Guidelines. If combinations/mixtures are intended, include qualifying language ('at least one member', 'or mixtures thereof'). Redundancy within the group does not necessarily render the claim indefinite (Eli Lilly v. Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush groups — breadth is not automatically indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim may encompass many alternatives and breadth alone does not make a claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the Markush group is so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention (e.g., an enormous chemical space), a rejection for indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate. Evaluate case-by-case (In re Gardner example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the term 'optionally' in alternative lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'optionally' (e.g., 'containing A, B, and optionally C') can be acceptable alternative language if there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu found 'optionally' acceptable where no ambiguity existed. If ambiguity arises because the list of potential alternatives can vary, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper and the examiner should explain the confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations are not inherently ambiguous; so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely, the claim complies with 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older criticisms exist (claims defining by what they are not), but courts have upheld negative limitations when definite (e.g., limitation 'free from the proteins...' in Wakefield; 'incapable of forming a dye...' in Barr). Any negative limitation must have basis in the original disclosure; absence of literal basis may not be sufficient for prima facie lack of descriptive support (Ex parte Parks). See MPEP §§ 2163-2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be rejected on the ground of 'old combination' following the 1952 Patent Act; such rejections are no longer valid as a separate doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be considered proper so long as they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph). Historical cases (Lincoln Engineering, Bernhart, Radio Steel) discussed; do not use 'old combination' as independent basis for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation' (non-statutory rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, see MPEP § 2172.01 for proper treatment. Evaluate whether rejection should instead be under a statutory ground (101/102/103/112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when long recitations or unimportant details render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prolix rejections apply where the metes and bounds cannot be determined due to lengthy, extraneous recitations; do not reject merely because claims are long—indefiniteness must result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity / undue multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented provided they differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied. Undue multiplicity (repetitious claims that confuse rather than clarify) may warrant rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rule of reason case-by-case (In re Chandler, In re Flint). Undue multiplicity rejections should be rare and applied judiciously. Examiner should contact applicant (telephone) to request selection of claims for examination; if applicant refuses, an undue multiplicity rejection of all claims should be made and the examiner should request selection in the next Office action. Procedure preserves appeal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule that double inclusion is improper; the governing consideration is what a reasonable construction of the claim language is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate facts of each case to determine whether multiple inclusion of one or more elements gives rise to indefiniteness. Double inclusion may be harmless in many Markush contexts but can cause indefiniteness in device claims if an element can be read to be included twice (Ex parte Kristensen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims (product claims defined in terms of the process by which they are made) are proper; a claim to a device, manufacture, or composition may include reference to the process in which it is intended to be used, so long as it is clear the claim is directed to the product and not the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma; In re Luck; In re Pilkington; In re Steppan. Applicant may present claims of varying scope even if product-by-process language is necessary (Ex parte Pantzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and process in same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus (product) and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims mixing statutory classes can create confusion as to when infringement occurs (Katz Interactive; IPXL Holdings). In contrast, claims that recite a product plus limitations focusing on system capabilities (not user actions) may be definite (Mastermine v. Microsoft).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Use' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps (mere 'use' recitation) generally raise indefiniteness issues under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may also fail 35 U.S.C. 101 because 'use' alone is not a statutory class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims reciting only a use ('a process for using X to isolate Y') found indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Use-claims that do not claim a statutory class may be rejected under 101 and/or 112. However, certain recited 'utilizing' steps were found not indefinite in particular contexts (Ex parte Porter). Examine whether steps are sufficiently recited and whether claim fits a statutory class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. See Ex parte Fressola (discussion of history and why omnibus claims do not comply). Use form paragraph 7.35; see MPEP § 2175.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to figures or tables in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words and incorporation is a necessity, not for applicant's convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Fressola cited; reference characters corresponding to elements in the drawings may be used with the recitation of the same element in the claims. Generally presence/absence of reference characters does not affect claim scope. See MPEP § 608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.
